shape.name: Shape F - Productive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional productive skills lesson with preparation stages followed by speaking or writing output.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Here the focus is on helping learners practice their speaking or writing skills. The lesson can usually be divided into preparation for speaking/writing and speaking/writing task stages.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to [speak/write] about [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to understand a for-and-against writing task and state a clear position on a technology topic with a reason and an example.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
06-08-26
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
F (Productive Skills - Writing)
Materials:
Slideshow, essay topic cards
Assessment:
Written response (position, reason, example)
Skills:
Writing, Speaking

stages.stage_aim: To activate students' prior knowledge of technology and opinions, and to introduce the Opinion-Reason-Evidence frame
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: "What do you see? An angel and a devil. What might this lesson be about?" Let students guess.
Advance to the title slide: "How can I express what I think about an issue?" Confirm the theme: today we start writing a for/against essay.
Show the "Why is this lesson important?" slide and read the bullets aloud.
Students work in pairs. Ask: "What technology do you use every day? What is good and bad about it?" Each student gives one reason. 2 minutes (timer).
Elicit two or three opinions. Point to the Opinion-Reason-Evidence line at the bottom of the slide.

stages.stage_aim: To teach students to read a for-and-against writing task and identify its three parts
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "The writing task."
Project the task on page 132. Read it aloud twice.
Teach the strategy table: read the task twice; every task has three parts.
Ask Exercise 1 on page 132: "What do you have to do in the essay?" Students answer from the task.
Reveal the answer slide row by row: both sides, then your opinion.

stages.stage_aim: To analyse the four-paragraph structure of the model essay and answer Exercises 2 and 3
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "The model essay."
Display the structure map: introduction, advantages, disadvantages, conclusion. Point at each paragraph on page 132.
Read the model essay together.
Work through Exercise 2 on page 132: the topic of the essay, and whether the writer is for or against, revealing each answer on click.
Work through Exercise 3 on page 132, one question at a time: number of paragraphs, paragraph openings, number of advantages, number of disadvantages, and the conclusion's contents.

stages.stage_aim: To show students that a good essay needs one clear opinion, and to model choosing a side
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Take a position."
Teach the strategy table: choose one side; your essay ends with your opinion; think about your own experience.
Show the teacher's example on the demo slide (weekend homework). Ask: "Which side would the teacher choose?"
Click to reveal the green check mark. Emphasise that no side is wrong, but students must choose one.

stages.stage: Your turn: read your topic card
stages.stage_aim: For students to apply the strategy to their own randomly assigned topic card
procedure: Show the red transition slide: "Your turn."
Distribute one essay topic card to each student at random. Students cannot choose their topic.
Project the task slide. Students read their question twice, find the technology, think of advantages and disadvantages, and choose their side.
Monitor and help students who cannot see both sides of their topic.

stages.stage_aim: For students to write a three-sentence response: position, reason, and example
procedure: Show the scaffold slide with the sentence frames: I am for/against ... , One reason is ... , For example, ...
Project the red task slide: "Write your response."
Students write three sentences: their position, one reason, and one example about their own topic card. 5 minutes (timer).
Collect the responses at the end of the stage.

stages.stage_aim: For students to share their position orally using the Opinion-Reason-Evidence frame
procedure: Show the discussion-structure slide with the Opinion-Reason-Evidence table and the weekend-homework example.
Students share their responses with a partner, using the frames: position, reason, example.
Elicit two or three strong examples for the whole class.
Show the wrap-up slide: "Your essay starts here." Preview lesson 2: planning the essay on pages 133-134.

shape.note: For middle schoolers interested in SCR approach to productive skills, see Shape J instead.

metadata.topic: For and against essays: understand the task, take a position
materials: Oxford Discover Futures 2, Unit "Writing workshop: A for and against essay", p. 132
Slideshow — Lesson 1: Understand the Task, Take a Position
Essay topic cards — 10 for-and-against topics, randomly distributed
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to understand a for-and-against writing task and state a clear position on a technology topic with a reason and an example.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also be better able to identify the four-paragraph structure of a for/against essay and the function of each paragraph.
answer_key: In the essay you give the advantages and disadvantages of a technology. You end with your own opinion and say whether you are for or against it.
1 The essay is about streaming music.
2 The writer is against streaming. The writer prefers downloads because it is much better to own the music you love.
1 There are four paragraphs: an introduction, two main paragraphs, and a conclusion.
2 Paragraph 2 begins with "Let's start with the advantages." Paragraph 3 begins with "Turning to the disadvantages, ..."

3 There are four advantages: you can listen anywhere on any device without using memory; you can create and share playlists; the choice is absolutely enormous; and it is possible to stream music for free.

4 There are four disadvantages: you need good Wi-Fi and a fairly big data allowance; the service can be expensive or the free service has annoying ads; the audio quality can be poor; and when you stream music, you don't own it at all.
5 The conclusion contains one advantage (the convenience of streaming) and the writer's opinion (it is much better to own the music you love; the writer still prefers downloads).
